Carcinoma is a term used in medicine to refer to any type of cancer that begins in abnormal cells. In the context of skin cancer, carcinoma refers specifically to squamous cell carcinoma and basal cell carcinoma, which are two main categories of nonmelanoma skin cancers (NMSCs).

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a type of NMSC that originates in the squamous cells, which are the flat, thin cells that make up the outer layer of the skin. SCC most often develops on sun-exposed areas of the body, such as the face, ears, and hands.

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC), on the other hand, is a type of NMSC that originates in the basal cells, which are the cells at the base of the epidermis, the outermost layer of the skin. BCC most often develops on sun-exposed areas of the body, such as the neck, face, and hands.

The American Cancer Society (ACS) states that over 100,000 new cases of melanoma will be diagnosed this year, and over 8,000 people will die from the disease. Melanoma is considered a serious form of skin cancer because it can spread to other parts of the body if left untreated.
